headline: GhostLock, a 15-year-old stack-UAF found in ALL Linux distributions
summary: The GhostLock vulnerability (CVE-2026-43499) allows unprivileged local attackers to achieve privilege escalation and container escape. It has affected every major Linux distribution since 2011, with a fix released in April 2026.
details: GhostLock (CVE-2026-43499), a critical Linux kernel vulnerability, has been found by VEGA, existing in every major distribution since 2011. It enables unprivileged local attackers to achieve 97% stable privilege escalation and container escape. Google rewarded VEGA $92,337 for its discovery in kernelCTF.

The bug was introduced in Linux 2.6.39 and remained unfixed for over 15 years until April 2026, when it was patched in Linux 7.1. All Linux distributions without the patch are affected and should consider upgrading to the latest LTS version. The affected range is v2.6.39-rc1 to v7.1-rc1.

The vulnerability stems from a misuse of the remove_waiter() helper function in kernel/locking/rtmutex.c. This function incorrectly assumes that current (the thread running) is always the waiter it needs to clean up, clearing current->pi_blocked_on accordingly.

However, with Requeue-PI, remove_waiter() is used on behalf of a different, sleeping thread. In this scenario, current is the thread that issued FUTEX_CMP_REQUEUE_PI, not the actual waiter. This leads to the waiter task retaining pi_blocked_on pointing to its own stack frame, which becomes a dangling pointer once the frame is popped.

Triggering the bug requires a PI dependency cycle built from three futex words and three threads, leading to an -EDEADLK rollback. This causes the waiter to wake with a dangling pi_blocked_on pointer, creating a Use-After-Free (UAF) window.

The UAF window remains wide open, allowing a follow-up sched_setattr() call to walk the dangling chain at any time. Exploiting this stack-UAF requires finding a syscall that can reclaim the freed object on the kernel stack with controlled bytes at the correct depth.

headline_marked: [[Boko Haram uses frontier AI]], according to Cambridge research
headline: Boko Haram uses frontier AI, according to Cambridge research
summary: A new report from the University of Cambridge's CASP program details how the terrorist group Boko Haram leverages advanced AI technologies. This research highlights critical implications for global security and policy.
details: The Cambridge Programme on AI Science & Policy (CASP) has released findings on the use of frontier AI by the terrorist organization Boko Haram. This interdisciplinary research from the University of Cambridge sheds light on a concerning trend in global security.

CASP's study investigates the specific applications of advanced artificial intelligence tools by the group. This includes potential uses in propaganda dissemination, recruitment strategies, and operational planning.

The research aims to inform policymakers and security experts about the evolving landscape of AI threats. Understanding these methods is crucial for developing countermeasures and mitigating risks posed by non-state actors.

This report underscores the dual-use nature of AI technologies, where powerful tools can be exploited for malicious purposes. It emphasizes the urgent need for robust governance and ethical frameworks around AI development and deployment.
